utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There are a few preliminary matters to be dealt with. Mr. Lukic, I think you still owe us a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. In regard of D899, we were instructed by the Chamber to inquire about the date and the place of this video. This video of ours is an excerpt from 65 ter 22615, which is uploaded as 65 ter exhibit by the Prosecution. The excerpt is marked as 1D03160. And it's only from the time of 14 minutes, 35 seconds, up to 16 minutes, 9 seconds from the same video. I spoke with Mr. Traldi and we concluded that the same video was taped -- actually, this part -- the whole video starts sometime before, but this part was taped on the 5th of August, 1992, since it's obvious that we can see Ms. Marshall in that video. So that's how we concluded that it has to be 5th of August, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's all we -- the Defence could discover by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Lukic. There were a few preliminary matters to be raised by the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: First, I have owed you for some time a response to your inquiry about the timing of the reopening, specifically with respect to May and June. In the interim, we have checked, and that timing presents no problem for the Prosecution with the tiny exception, and that is if the Court wanted to begin in May and run without interruption to the conclusion of the reopening, there might be a scheduling issue with one witness who was not available, I think, in the first week and third week of May but is available in June. So if that wasn't particularly a concern, we could commence in May. And even if we didn't find ourselves with a sufficient window in May for that witness, we'd pick him up again in June. But in any event, that's the status. So May and June is fine. Secondly, I wanted to respond in connection with the Defence request for an adjournment at Easter. As a general matter, the Prosecution takes no position on that and leaves it to the Chamber. It did occur to us, however, that there was one aspect of scheduling that did not implicate the concerns about disrupting witnesses' Easter and could nevertheless go forward, and that is with respect to two remaining videolinks in the Banja Luka area. It occurred to the Prosecution that if those, for example, were scheduled on the Friday of the week that is proposed for the adjournment, it wouldn't require the witnesses to travel on or about Easter, which seemed to the basis of Mr. Lukic's concern. They could remain in situ and the videolinks could take place on Friday. The only people travelling presumably would be those who would not concerned about -- or at least as much concerned about the timing of the holiday. Now, that's not to take a position one way or another as I say. It seems to me that, one way or the another, that's a useful scheduling issue to bear in mind, but it seemed particularly pertinent to note in light of the matter the Court is currently considering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Lukic, especially in relation to the last point, any comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I spoke with Mr. Tieger this morning, and I said that we will try to do whatever is possible to have this arranged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the Chamber is still considering your request, so therefore it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And regarding the first topic, the reopening of the OTP case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think its obvious and everybody is aware the Defence did not have time to deal with this new case of the Prosecution or new part of the case by the Prosecution, so we will file our -- now when we have the position of the OTP that May and June is not a problem for them, then we will have to ask for an interruption of trial and we'll ask for some time to be given to the Defence to prepare for this segment so -- since we did not have time to work on that segment at all by now. And it requires -- first of all, technically we have to ask the Registry to allow us to have extra expert witnesses, for example, to respond to the OTP. But first we have to see what there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this matter is pending now for such a long time. If you make any further submissions, the Chamber would also like to know exactly what you've done until now to -- I mean, the experts are known for ages. Some of the experts are well known as far as their expertise is concerned, et cetera. So therefore, the Chamber wonders what anticipatory action you've taken until today, because you could expect that it would be somewhere around this time. Otherwise, to put such a matter at the end of the Defence case, of course, was not what was intended by either the Prosecution or would not be expected by the Defence, I would say. So therefore, make your submissions, Mr. Lukic, but also make clear what you've done until now, because asking for a postponement just on the basis of what still has to be done if all opportunities -- if opportunities have been missed what could have been done, that is still a matter to be considered. I leave it to that for the time being. I don't draw any conclusions. I'm just pointing at what the Chamber would like to know if you make further submissions asking for a postponement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, I just wanted to add that the opportunities have not been missed. We do not have manpower to deal with anything else but with the Defence case we are dealing right now. We don't have means at all to deal with something extra. All our efforts are only in align with providing the Defence witnesses for this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So all our staff is succumbed. And you could notice that even in January we missed several dead-lines because we were not able to follow the trial itself in the speed it goes, and we did not have time to deal with the reopening of the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, if we will spend time on hearing the reopening of the Prosecution's case, that means that for that period of time you will not have to prepare for the witnesses you had in mind earlier to present during that period of time. I mean, they will be postponed as well. So part of your burden on your shoulders will be postponed as a consequence of hearing the Prosecution's case. But again, this is not, perhaps, the best moment to discuss it in detail. But I just wanted to draw your attention to what may be considered relevant by the Chamber. We'll hear further submissions. Thank you. If there are no further preliminaries, could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Perhaps I could already deal with one matter briefly. The Chamber understands that the Defence still needs to file five expert reports: Two drafted by ballistic experts, one by a historian, one by a forensic pathologist, and finally, one drafted by a radio communications expert. Is the Defence in a position to provide the Chamber and the Prosecution with an update on the drafting and the filing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from you later today. Good morning, Mr. Solaja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Solaja, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And Mr. Traldi will now continue his cross-examination. Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, esteemed Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Could we have 65 ter 32144.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, what we see here is an interview with General Talic authored by yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 2 in the English and the first column of page 1 in the B/C/S, the first bolded question, if we could zoom in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see you ask General Talic about Operation Corridor, and I have some very short questions about this exchange. First, in your question you refer to what you describe as a monstrous intention to cut off the majority of Serbs from their motherland. By "their motherland" you mean Serbia; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in his answer beginning in the fifth line of that answer in the English, General Talic says: "Our people have succeeded in something that eluded numerous generations from the battle of Kosovo to the present day. They secured a unified living space for the Serbian people." And General Talic is speaking of the territory controlled by the VRS as a living space for Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And he says in the next sentence that this was a decisive operation for the Serbian people in the Krajinas who had been separated from the motherland and threatened with complete annihilation. First, when he refers to the "Krajinas," plural, he's referring to both the Bosnian Krajina and the Knin Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is no other.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And second, it's right, isn't it, that Krajiski Vojnik published articles asserting that the Serbian people in the ARK and in the Knin Krajina were threatened with complete annihilation and fighting for their very survival; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender 65 ter 32144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32144 receives number P7191.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I want to turn now, sir, to events in Banja Luka. First, you discuss the departures of Croats and Muslims from Banja Luka in your statement, and you say those were organised by civilian authorities and the VRS did not participate in that process. In fact, the 1st Krajina Corps' view was that the civilian authorities should work harder at the departure of the Croatian and Muslim population from Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, can P --

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never had such instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have P3714. This is a daily combat report by the 1st Krajina Corps dated the 28th of July, 1992. If we could have page 2 in the B/C/S but stay on page 1 in the English. Sorry, if we could have the next page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Under point 3, we read: "In the city of Banja Luka and other large towns, there is an increased demand for, and organisation of, the departure of Croatian and Muslim population. We consider that the municipal and regional authorities should work much harder at this." Now, that was the 1st Krajina Corps' position, that the regional and municipal authorities should work much harder at organising these departures, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was not accessible to me. It is one of the confidential documents that we never had access to, but no one ever gave us an instruction like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the Chamber has received evidence that during the war tens of thousands of Muslims and Croats left Banja Luka municipality. You're aware of that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I want to turn now to your discussion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Solaja, part of the problem may be that you were asked what the view of the 1st Krajina Corps was, and your answer was: "No, we never had such instructions." Now, you were not asked about receiving instructions but you were asked about the views of the Krajina Corps. Now, if you don't know or if you have not complete information, please tell us that you may not have known the views of the 1st Krajina Corps, because there is a -- the question and the answer do not connect very well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is in this document is one of the regular daily papers that circulated in the chain of command, and such information was not presented to us, and nothing else was binding upon us except for an official position which was never given to us in that way. We never knew that, we never had instructions like that, that we would write about something like that, and that can be seen from the content of the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which means that you may not have had access to complete information to answer this question with every detail. Mr. Traldi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I want to turn now to your evidence about the civilian authorities in the Banja Luka area. The Trial Chamber has received evidence about the rhetoric used by some members of the civilian authorities in the ARK, particularly Mr. Brdjanin. You were aware, for instance, that Brdjanin had said in public that only a thousand elderly Muslims could stay in Banja Luka to sweep the streets; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I wasn't there at that most critical point in time. I heard something like that, but I cannot say that I heard it myself. I couldn't even follow the media because of lack of physical contact. The 28th of July, I wasn't there until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You remained in Banja Luka. That's where you were based for the rest of the war after that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was born there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received evidence that in 1994 - and I'm referring to P6976 - at a rally, Mr. Brdjanin announced or stated in pertinent part that non-Serbs were befouling Serb soil. You're aware of statements like that that he continued to make while you were in Banja Luka; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a party rally. I remember that. I did not belong to the party. I didn't participate in that. At the same time, people who lived in Republika Srpska -- well, it was almost impossible for them to move somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you don't mention Mr. Brdjanin or his rhetoric in your statement; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had no contact with him. He represented the civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you do mention Predrag Radic. And in paragraph 34 of your statement, you assert that Radic wanted to keep Muslims from leaving Banja Luka. I have a few questions in this regard. But first, it's correct, isn't it, that you have mentioned the views of a political leader who, in your understanding, wanted to keep the Muslims from leaving, you have not included in your statement the views of political leaders who were calling for the Muslims to leave; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. That's because I had very good contacts on a personal level with Mr. Radic, and I knew his positions very well and I referred to them in this statement, not only in terms of the departure of Muslims, Croats too, and also his position that after the war the area of the former Yugoslavia would be linked up once again in the economic field and in other fields, which is indeed what happened. As for other civilian representatives, I didn't have that much contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, your view of Mr. Radic based on those contacts was that he was an honourable man; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And your view was that he was an honest man; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received evidence from Mr. Radic in the form of his testimony in the Krajisnik case, and he stated, for instance, that President Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik had blamed him for not having expelled non-Serbs from Banja Luka, that that left too many non-Serbs remaining there to feed and give medical care. Were you aware of those positions of the Republika Srpska leadership relative to Mr. Radic's attitude towards non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was under constant pressure from people who were at the political top and who were more radical, and he tried to soften the situation. I don't know about concrete events and concrete rhetoric, but I know that he had problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: When you say people at the political top, who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean many people from the region and from the republic who were not satisfied with his approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of the people from the republic level you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I didn't really deal with this in depth. I knew that there were these tensions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Mr. Radic's evidence was that because of these pressures, he couldn't openly assist non-Serbs even if he would have wanted to. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what he said. But he did help. He helped in a great many specific cases. That was the way in which he was able to help, because the pressure was pretty big and he didn't dare speak about this openly. This was a time of war and these democratic methods did not always work in favour of people who implemented them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you referred to the destruction of mosques in your statement. His evidence was that members of the Bosnian Serb leadership and their emissaries had criticised him because the mosques in Banja Luka were still standing. Were you also aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, in this context, sir, you describe --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And I have no more questions on that topic, unless the Chamber does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I -- there is one item I'd like to briefly address. You said you were very close to Mr. Radic. He told that he was blamed by Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic. He never told you who they were that criticised him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It was better not to publish or announce such issues in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But if you were close to him, he may have told you, Well, this is what happens, but don't publish it, which is not uncommon in the journalistic world, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we were not doing it for professional reasons. This was a purely private contact. Because it was impossible to have something like that published at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Krajina Soldier, we did publish some criticism including that against the very leadership of Republika Srpska. I may mention the interview of the minister for veterans issues, Dragan Djokanovic, who openly criticised Radovan Karadzic about certain issues. However, due to issues of personal security this was quite limited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's exactly for that reason - you said, I was close, it was all private conversations - that I sought verification that Mr. Radic never told you that this blame was expressed by Mr. Karadzic and/or by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Probably he wanted to protect others, not only me, and that was probably the reason that he didn't talk about this openly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It also means, does it, that you have no reason to have any doubt if Mr. Radic later told us that or told us that he gave statements or testimony that it was at the level of Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik? You have no reason to doubt the accuracy of such information, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't doubt his statements. He was a very honourable man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sticking with the topic of the civilian authorities in Banja Luka, you described the disbanding of the ARK Crisis Staff in paragraphs 26 through 28 of your statement. Now, after the ARK Crisis Staff was abolished, its members who held high positions in the government and the army all kept their jobs; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you say in paragraph 27 that Miro Mladjenovic, the author of Glas, asked you to help have the Crisis Staff abolished and you published an article in this regard. In fact, immediately after the article you published, Mladjenovic was fired as editor of Glas; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that was for some quite different reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staffs did not have any impact on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That decision was taken by the ARK War Presidency and confirmed by the Banja Luka Municipal Assembly; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as the official founder of this paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the president of the ARK War Presidency, do you recall who that was?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the ARK had a government. It had the assembly and the government but not a War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, the president of the assembly was Vojo Kupresanin; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the vice-president, who was that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32201.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just want to inquire, is this document on the list?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We sent an updated list Friday specifically calling attention in our e-mail to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And on the right of the page in the B/C/S, we see an article called: "How to Remove the Traces?" It's headlined: "Banja Luka, 10 July." And it starts: "Two high-ranking AR Krajina officials, Vojo Kupresanin, Assembly President, and Radoslav Brdjanin, Vice-President, held a selective press conference yesterday inviting to it only broadcasting media, Banja Luka Radio, and Banja Luka Television." First, does that refresh your recollection as to the vice-president of the assembly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now it does. But still I don't have this perception that it was Brdjanin, because mostly it was Mr. Kupresanin who was at the fore.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Well, we see related to Mr. Kupresanin's role, we see Mr. Brdjanin speak about that at what I think is the bottom of the column in the B/C/S, and he says, among other things: "A minister of information in the AR Krajina government will be appointed very soon, and until then his duties will be performed by Vojo Kupresanin who I am sure will make a marvellous job of it." Had Mladjenovic previously served as minister of information in the ARK?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, he did. But there is something else. The government of the ARK was never completed. It only had four ministries where everyone was appointed. I don't know exactly which ones they were, but I know that it was never really complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And Mr. Kupresanin and Mr. Brdjanin, they were both members of the ARK Crisis Staff; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Brdjanin, and I'm not sure about Kupresanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So what I'm putting to you is: The members of the ARK Crisis Staff, as you testified, kept their high positions in the government and the army, Mladjenovic was fired, and these are important parts of understanding the abolition of the Crisis Staff that you have not informed the Chamber of in your statement. You've not provided a full picture of those events. That's the truth, right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not involved nor did I particularly follow the events that had to do both with the ARK Krajina and also what happened after the Crisis Staff had been abolished. The Crisis Staff came into existence because some people became its members due to their official positions, but there was a great danger that it might become a power outside of the system. That was the reason why I personally participated as a journalist in leaving out something that's not part of the system from the decision-making process. I think that we succeeded in this and that it was very useful for that period. Let me remind you that Republika Srpska itself came into existence after the decision or, rather, the process in which three ethnic groups could not reach an agreement about the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was just the beginning of the creation of institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to interrupt you. You've gone well beyond the question I asked. I just have one question to follow-up on your answer. Is it your evidence that somehow the ARK Crisis Staff, which included the highest leaders of the ARK Assembly, the 1st Krajina Corps commander, and the head of CSB Banja Luka, that this was somehow an institution that wasn't part of the system? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32201 receives number P7192.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Next, sir, you say there were no camps in Banja Luka for Muslims and Croats and then you discuss Manjaca. The people detained in Manjaca were Muslims and Croats obviously; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But when I say in Banja Luka, I mean that there were no camps founded by the institutions of Banja Luka town. And Manjaca was a prison for prisoners of war and it was organised by the Army of Republika Srpska. So in the legal sense, it was not important where it was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I have a few follow-up questions on Manjaca, specifically. Now, you say in your statement the camp was closed in November 1992. It's a small point, but actually December 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in December or perhaps late November. I remember that it really wasn't so cold, so perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 32032.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, this is a letter from Radovan Karadzic to Daniel Schiffer, who you mention in your statement. In the first paragraph, President Karadzic refers to the visit by Elie Wiesel that you also mention in your statement. And in pertinent part we read in the middle of the third paragraph: "In honour of Mr. Wiesel and his associates' visit to Yugoslavia and the Republic of Srpska and on the occasion of our Orthodox Christmas, we are willing to release all prisoners from Manjaca if the international community and the ICRC are ready to accept them and convey them to third countries." The Bosnian Serb leadership conditioned closing Manjaca on the conveyance of those detainees who were released to third countries; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender 65 ter 32032 [Realtime transcript read in error "30232"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 32032 receives number P7193.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning now to Prijedor --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I think there may be -- I think the number may be mis-recorded at page 19, line 9. The P number for the last document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The number should be P7193.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning now to Prijedor, were you ever deployed to Prijedor yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You never --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I clarify if the 65 ter number is correct. We have two versions, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: The second time at page 19, line 7, I'm recorded as having said 65 ter 30232 and I intended, at least, to have said 32032, as I did when I called it up. I apologise for any ambiguity I may have created there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then we have now 32032 in evidence as P7193.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: You just said you were never deployed to Prijedor yourself. You never participated in any combat there; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. I never was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you never served in the 5th or the 43rd Brigade of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: So in paragraph 46 when you say: "There was no organised deployment of soldiers in Prijedor," you have no idea whether that's true or not, do you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I see paragraph 46, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: It's the last paragraph of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the commander of the communications platoon, I was in an artillery unit, which was much bigger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The statement of the witness is D924.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That unit included soldiers from all areas of the Bosnian Krajina including, inter alia, from Prijedor. We were deployed to the south of the Banja Luka when this rebellion broke out in Prijedor and the fighting in Prijedor broke out. Most of the soldiers from Prijedor did not ask for permission. They just took their weapons and of their own initiative set out towards Prijedor with the explanation that their families were there. That was not allowed. However, their motive was so strong that no one was able to stop them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, just to be very specific, what I'm putting to you is when you say there was no organised deployment of soldiers in Prijedor, there was no military order in that respect, what you're aware of is the behaviour of a number of soldiers in the rocket brigade. You have no personal knowledge as to the brigades that were based in Prijedor or as to any of the events -- the military events in Prijedor except for this event at the end of May; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any other information except for this departure of soldiers of their own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, we left off Friday with -- sorry, Thursday, with your visit to Prijedor. I will focus on that visit for the rest of your testimony. First, you mention that you went to Omarska. You were aware, because you and the press centre --

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a part of a group of journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, because you and the press centre kept track of international media, as you testified Thursday, you were aware that there had been reporting about terrible conditions in Omarska and other camps before your visit; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those reports were very superficial, and this was discussed more as rumour and rumours than any sort of evidence. Actually, we heard most of this after Radovan Karadzic had attended the London Conference where there was more talk about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, I understand your answer to be: Yes, you were aware there had been reporting about terrible conditions in the camps before your visit; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew very little and we did not have any real evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Trial Chamber has received evidence that the 1st Krajina Corps command knew at the time you went that before your visit, more than a thousand prisoners had been transported from Omarska to Manjaca and some of them had been murdered outside Manjaca camp. Were you, like the 1st Krajina Corps command, aware of those events?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know it at the time. I heard something about this later.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you know as you sit there today, this is in the context of almost all the prisoners at Omarska being transported from Omarska to Manjaca before your visit; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: About how many prisoners did you see at Omarska when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a full picture because we only passed through the restaurant where they were being served their lunch at that moment, and it was impossible to make an estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you were aware that on the previous journalists' visit to Omarska, they'd been stopped from recording certain things; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that at the time. But this was a short time, only two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And did you see any elderly prisoners when you were there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Any that were ill?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But the visit itself was very short, so I didn't have an opportunity to pay much attention to details. We were going to a press conference that was to be held by Mr. Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you also mention visits to Manjaca. You're aware that there was a journalists' visit to Manjaca on about the same day, and the prisoners who'd been transferred from Omarska the journalists weren't allowed to see; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know this because this was all happening at Manjaca and I wasn't present. So I wasn't aware of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received evidence that your immediate superior, Lieutenant-Colonel Milutinovic, was part of that visit. He didn't tell you that the reporters weren't allowed to see the prisoners who had been transferred from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't tell me, personally. But I can't remember whether we discussed that at all, because we were not there at the time. So probably I missed out on that or there may have been other reasons, but I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And you said Thursday you went to Keraterm yourself. Which parts of the camp did you go to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, only one front section where Colonel Arsic took us and where there was really nothing at all. Some journalists even moved some boxes and looked around, but they never found anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, the Chamber has received evidence that the 1st Krajina Corps command was aware that about two weeks earlier there had been a massacre of prisoners at Keraterm camp. Were you aware of that yourself?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the journalists weren't taken to the rooms where the prisoners had previously been detained, were they?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in what rooms the prisoners were detained. This was the only occasion when I went to Keraterm and when we were all together in a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And so they weren't taken into any rooms, for instance, that had bullet holes in the door and in the wall above them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am about to turn to a document. I have, I think, about 10 to 15 minutes of questions remaining. Looking at the clock, I think it might be best to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we take a break first. Mr. Solaja, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. We would like to see you back after that break. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We -- Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President. It's a Monday morning thing, I'm afraid. If I could offer one quick clarification about the point I earlier made concerning the Banja Luka videolink issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's simply that those are witnesses for whom the Defence indicated it intended to make a motion for videolink and I may have inadvertently suggested that the videolink issue had already been resolved. So all of that was assuming that, in fact, the motion was made and there was a sufficient basis for granting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you're suggesting that scheduling them on, for example, a Friday or at least later on in this week might accommodate some of the concerns the Defence has in calling -- in having witnesses available to testify?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That part was still correct. But again, it assumes the underlying initial bases are met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's hereby on the record. Thank you for that. And we resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we have 65 ter 03327.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And what we see here is headlined: "Press Release." We see at the top: "Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Government," and the date, the 7th of August, 1992. And we see at the beginning that it responds to a CNN broadcast of the 6th of August about the situation of those imprisoned in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Except it's talking about 1882 instead of 1992, the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sorry, the English does say "1882" and the B/C/S "1992." We'll have that checked. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Turning to page 4 in the English and 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see that it bears Prime Minister Djeric's name at the bottom. And in the second paragraph in the English, we read: "It is undeniable that rooms in Omarska are not equipped for the stay of large number of persons and that there are not enough sanitary and other equipment." Now, you were aware, weren't you, that on the day of the your visit, the government of the Republika Srpska was conceding that previously there'd been too many prisoners in Omarska for what the space and the sanitary facilities allowed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government stated its views on the matter, but what I see in this document looks like a draft to me rather than a document as such. I've never seen it. But I see that something was crossed out, several paragraphs, so I cannot assert that this is a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it is a document, but you may have some doubts as to what it stands for, whether it's a final document, whether it's a draft, but -- Witness, but, I think, the question was whether you were aware that on the day of your visit, the government of Republika Srpska was conceding that previously there'd been too many prisoners in Omarska. Do you have any knowledge about that apart from your comments on this document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We cannot hear the witness. Could all other microphones please be switched off when the witness is speaking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you repeat your answer, whether you were aware of the government, the Republika Srpska government conceding this previous situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, from the media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: We see below that that the press release states that the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina had issued an order, according to this release, to "immediately release from Omarska persons older than 60 years of age, heavily wounded, and sick persons, except for those against whom urgent criminal procedures were ordered ..." Were you also aware from the media that before your visit, elderly people, heavily wounded people, and sick people, among others, had been kept as prisoners in Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And the fact that elderly people, heavily wounded people, sick people, were among the people transferred from Omarska to Manjaca before your visit, that was part of the reason that journalists weren't allowed to see the Omarska prisoners on their first Manjaca visit; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not in the media, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 03327 receives number P7194.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7194 is admitted. Witness, your last answer was, and it's not the first time, you said: "That was not in the media, either." The questions always seek any personal knowledge you may have or hearsay evidence, not whether something was in the media. So therefore, could you please answer that question now; that is, that the fact that elderly people, heavily wounded people, sick people were among the people transferred from Omarska to Manjaca before your visit, that that was part of the reason that journalists weren't allowed to see the Omarska prisoners on their first Manjaca visit. Could you please answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: I'm going to turn to Trnopolje now, sir, finally, and I'm going to ask Ms. Stewart to play a video with 65 ter 22393c.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: For the record, I should note we'll play it twice to allow the translation to be confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "For Trnopolje has changed. There's now some food getting through, although the queues are long, and there is also shelter and clothes provided by the Serbian authorities. And the barbed wire fence which shocked the world has been torn down from its posts. All this has been done in advance of the simultaneous arrival of the Red Cross and our cameras. For certain, conditions here have improved. These refugees are safer. But the Red Cross have still not been allowed to enter any other camps and our visits are closely supervised."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: "For Trnopolje has changed. There is now some food getting through, although the queues are long, and there is also shelter and clothes provided by the Serbian authorities. And the barbed wire fence which shocked the world has been torn down from its posts. All this has been done in advance of the simultaneous arrival of the Red Cross and our cameras. For certain, conditions here have improved. These refugees are safer. But the Red Cross have still not been allowed to enter any other camps and our visits are closely supervised."

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Now, you say in your statement there was no barbed wire at Trnopolje. You know from having monitored foreign media about events in the ARK that barbed wire had been taken down in advance of the journalists' visit that you were on; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see a wire and I don't know of its existence. And I haven't seen it in this footage, and I'd like to know when this footage was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What I'm putting to you, sir, is you know there was barbed wire on the previous visit. When you say in your statement there was none on the visit that you were on, that you didn't see any barbed wire, what you're describing is preparations to present a more acceptable image of the camp; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First, asked and answered. The gentleman said what he knew. Second, this gentleman asked my colleague when this recording was taken, and I think it is a legitimate question and he should be provided first with that data.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was partly asked, but something at least was added to it -- asked, and to some extent answered. To the limited extent it was asked, there was an answer. But Mr. Traldi now adds something to it, that is, what the witness is describing in his statement and puts to him what it is in the view of the Prosecution. So to that extent the question is admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please, Mr. Lukic. And, Mr. Traldi, I think if you are putting to the witness that he is describing preparations to present a more acceptable image, if you would give a time-frame to that it might make it easier for the witness to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sure. I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Sir, you're aware from your monitoring of the international press that journalists had filmed barbed wire on their previous visit to Trnopolje. What I'm putting to you is that the fact there was no barbed wire when this footage was filmed, the fact you did not see barbed wire on your visit, reflect the results of preparations after that first visit on the 5th, before your visit on the 7th, to present a more acceptable image of Trnopolje camp to the world. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know of any wire around Trnopolje before the 5th or on the 5th. I just know that in part there was an old fence that could have been interpreted as such a wire. But as far as I know, there was no fence. Even the foreign media, and we followed their subsequent reports too, there was no mention of a wire. It would be a good thing if we have full footage of this wire, if that is what is being claimed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has seen most of that footage, so therefore we'll not necessarily play it again. We are aware of the discussion about some of the wire that was shown on other parts of the footage. Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd tender this clip.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is now for the second time seeking to consult counsel with a loud voice, so if he could speak at a lower volume, that would be preferred. Madam Registrar, the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 22393c receives number P7195.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7195 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: And, sir, what I'm putting to you is: At Keraterm, these journalists weren't taken to the room that had recently been a massacre site; at Omarska, most of the prisoners had been removed; at Trnopolje, the barbed wire was gone. What I'm putting to you is: This visit was a propaganda exercise designed to undermine or conceal the truth that had been recently reported about the terrible criminal conditions in these camps. That's the truth about this visit; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The visit was agreed by President Karadzic, as far as I know, in London, with foreign representatives. And I don't know why they agreed to it if they considered it to be propaganda. I just know with this group because that's when I did the same work as all other journalists who were there. There were many foreign media that were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Traldi. Before we -- no, Mr. Lukic, if you have any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Solaja. Good day once again.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will just briefly go through some of the topics that were raised by my colleague, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P7191. We're going to start with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In this text, General Talic speaks about the corridor, the establishment of the corridor, its importance. This Chamber has heard evidence about those 12 babies that died because of a lack of oxygen. Do you have any personal knowledge about that time and about that occurrence or, rather, these occurrences; namely, the deaths of these babies? Just tell us whether you know and then I'm going to put other questions if you do know about it.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was intervention sought to have oxygen provided to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was asked for was having oxygen transported by plane from Belgrade to Banja Luka. However, at that time, what was valid was a UN resolution on a no-fly zone, so the UN did not allow this plane to fly from Belgrade to Banja Luka. Dr. Ilic was the director of the hospital at that time, and he personally asked the president of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Alija Izetbegovic, and he also tried to speak to the president of Croatia, Franjo Tudjman. However, oxygen was not provided to Banja Luka because Banja Luka at that point in time - that is to say, Bosanski Brod, Modrica, Doboj, Knin - this entire area had been cut off from the rest of the world, physically.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether everything has been recorded. What was the answer of Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no answer. That's what Dr. Ilic claims in the film that was made dealing with that topic, because the thirteenth baby survived, though seriously damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was Alija Izetbegovic asked to do?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To help make this decision, that the plane with the oxygen be brought to Banja Luka. And not only oxygen but also other kinds of medicine. What was the name of that for kidney treatment? Dialysis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now let us look at P3714, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for it, Witness, where does all this knowledge come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That part, I mean, of then Bosanska Krajina and the Republic of Serb Krajina was physically separated. And I lived there at the time, I was injured, and they had to transport me by bicycle to a doctor. There was no fuel. There was no food and many other things that were needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. My question was about where do you have your detailed knowledge about who said what in relation to the oxygen problem. Where -- you know that -- who -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I learned that two years ago from this film, "A Breath of Life," that was made and that dealt with that topic, and this Dr. Ilic is a witness who speaks about that. And the then Secretary-General, Boutros Boutros-Ghali took part in that, and I gave the final assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, indeed we've heard evidence about the event. And now to invite the witness to summary what he learned two years ago from a television programme or from a film is not what assists the Chamber. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I knew about that earlier, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you about when you learned about it. You said two years ago. But you have no direct knowledge yourself --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is reliable evidence. Yes, I had direct information from Dr. Ilic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then why didn't you tell us before when I said what your -- where does your knowledge come from? When did you meet Dr. Ilic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we worked together at the time. In the 1990s, I worked in this health system as an advisor. However, I thought that public information was more reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's not for you to make an assessment of the reliability of the evidence. It is for you to tell us what your personal knowledge and experience was. This also sheds some further light --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having cautioned me. I really don't have any experience with courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's understood. Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, did the media report about that?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. It made the headlines. However, the media did not get very far. At that time, there was no electricity, so people would listen to the news on small transistor radios and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P3714, please. Could we have that now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: According to the transcript you asked for 3794 previously but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 3714.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: "14." Then it's perhaps not recorded well on page 33, line 23. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was also shown to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 2 in the English version and page 3 in B/C/S. So it is a document of the command of the 1st Krajina Corps, dated the 28th of July, 1992. [In English] I'm sorry, I will need previous page in English version. We need number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, you were asked about number 3 here, and it says: "In the city of Banja Luka and other large towns there is an increased demand for, and organisation of, the departure of the Croatian and Muslim population." Do you know who these requests for departures came from?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think from citizens of Croat and Muslim ethnicity. They applied because I think many were afraid. This fear was a fear for basic existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And do you know anything about this way in which it was organised? Could it be unorganised? How could one leave Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In an unorganised manner, it was absolutely impossible because until the corridor was broken through, we were absolutely sealed off on all sides. And the fear of death was the fear that there would be lack of food, because they did not care about Serbs or Croats or Muslims or anyone. There was only the possibility to move through the corridor, along it towards Serbia or via Gradiska and into Croatia. That was the only way.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have a look at P6976.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One follow-up question. Do you have any explanation as to why the document only talks about the Croatian and the Muslim population and its departure? Does that mean that the Serbs had no fear for their lives at that time in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was fear, too. But Serbs were not allowed to leave. They could only do that illegally or somehow sidestepping what was usual and to get the proper papers, because Republika Srpska had said that it had the competence in this territory. But it did not force Muslims and Croats to serve the army. It was just that some of them were doing that voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And Serbs are not allowed to leave on the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was not possible to travel freely, and everyone was obliged in accordance with the laws of Republika Srpska to participate in the work of institutions. One of the institutions was the army, which mobilised the Serbs into the army because it was wartime and conscription was compulsory even though the state of war as such had not yet been officially declared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But that's perhaps for those who were under a duty to -- under the mobilisation, but this is about Croatians, Muslims, the population, and I asked you about the Serbs, not about those Serbs fit for military service. They could not travel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means women, elderly, youngsters, they could not -- they were not allowed to travel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only those who had to travel on business or if they needed treatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, Croats and Muslims, were they allowed to travel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Freely? No. They requested to be allowed to leave and go to third countries. But they were not forced to request this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It all still doesn't explain why this daily combat report is focusing on Croats and Muslims, whereas you say Serbs couldn't travel either. I mean, I'm seeking explanation why this document is not talking about population that wishes to leave but is talking about Croats and Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Serbs didn't submit their requests to leave so frequently, or they didn't submit them at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was living there at the time. I mean, I've been living there all my life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to continue with the topic without asking any leading questions. What was the manner in which a Serb could leave and go to Serbia? What did he need?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had to have a strong reason because Serbia also had an immigration policy that did not allow for people to move there freely. It had to be either treatment or business or some similar reason and some kind of need had to exist that could not be resolved in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was it necessary to have some documents?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were special permits which were issued for such occasions because the system with the use of passports did not function. No one could issue passports because Republika Srpska had not been internationally recognised. So that was the limiting factor which prevented Serbs from leaving. Only specific documents could be used that worked in specific situations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now look at P6976, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Here in this document, Mr. Brdjanin also speaks later. My learned friend showed you this. However, here on page 1, we see that it's Mr. Radic who is the speaker. You have told us that he was an honourable man, a person of integrity. He says here, that's approximately around line 7, from where we can see that he starts to speak, and he says: "The victims of this war are our children. The victims of the last war were our brothers, sisters, fathers, and mothers. The victims of the war before that one were our fathers and grandfathers, and of the one still before, our grandfathers and great-grandfathers. They all had one goal: to live in large numbers and graced by God, with their own people and nothing more, recognising that other peoples have the same right." Having reported and worked for the newspaper for which you did work, did you ever have an opportunity to hear anyone tell you to spread propaganda to the effect that other people should not live together with Serbs in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we never received any such instructions. I even think that Republika Srpska declared itself as a civil society, a civil state. I think that the preamble to the constitution reads that the constitution is adopted by the Serbs and other ethnicities living in Republika Srpska. I think that was the original version of the constitution and that this was in its preamble.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see here that the date is 21st August 1994. It's a broadcast of the rally of the Serbian unit in Banja Luka. After two years of war, Mr. Radic says that the same right is recognised to other peoples, the same one that the Serbs have. Do you know that he changed that position by the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He never did. That was, among other things, the reason that on the 2nd of January, 1996, President Bill Clinton received him as one of the most mild politicians in Republika Srpska, or perhaps the one who was the least hardened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's look briefly at 65 ter 11306. I don't know if this has been admitted already. We did talk about abolished Crisis Staffs. We need in English page 3, paragraph 2. And in the B/C/S version, we need the third column, the second paragraph. If we could zoom in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This has to do with the press conference of the defence minister of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Colonel Bogdan Subotic, published in Glas on the 7th of July, 1992. So that was more or less at the beginning of the war. At the beginning of the second paragraph, in the third column, it reads: [As read] "All citizens who accept the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as their own state will remain within its borders and will enjoy all civil rights." The author of the report from this press conference is M. Solaja.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To whom was this addressed? Who was reading Glas?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Glas was a paper that had 50 years of tradition behind itself, and it was normally sold on newsstands. So everyone was reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the "Krajina Soldier"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The "Krajina Soldier" was the paper of the 1st Krajina Corps and it was distributed among units, but it could also be bought at newsstands. So it was distributed in the retail network.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the main population that was reading the "Krajina Soldier"?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyone who got it, but it was intended primarily for the soldiers of the 1st Krajina Corps, but not in the sense of propaganda but as an information bulletin that would convey information about the most important events. That was our concept. Because we believed that there was no need to spread propaganda among our own troops but rather that they should be told the truth. So it was the idea to convey realistically the facts about what was going on. We were not political propagandists, but we just wanted to report about the topical events of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please have a look at P7912 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering the last document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will tender that document. It was on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document 11306 receives number D925.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D925 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Lukic, can you just check the number that you have just called? You said 79 ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I asked for 7192.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, that's better.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am showing you this document just to refresh your memory about the topic. It had to do with the replacement of the editor-in-chief of the Glas paper. On transcript page 17, line 12, you started talking about the fact that Republika Srpska had just been created after the process in which the three ethnic groups could not reach an agreement about the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I heard, but it has not been recorded, that you said that. Do you remember what you said further on about the initial stage of creation of institutions?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if I may continue. The federal system of the Yugoslav institutions had broken down, and the internal system of institutions of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina also broke down. In a part of the territory, there were self-organised local organs, and on the basis of that Republika Srpska came into existence and it defined itself on the basis of constitution from 1992. So ARK and Crisis Staffs were this interim stage until the proper functioning of normal institutions was established.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. And now the editor-in-chief of Glas was relieved of his duty. What was the reason for his replacement? Did it have anything to do with the abolishment of Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, as far as I remember, though I wasn't really involved in that. I think that these were internal political reasons and that they didn't have anything to do with Crisis Staffs or any other events at the time. Because there were quite a few such similar replacements even later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could the witness -- could you tell us then, what was the reason? What was the internal -- what were the internal problems? Could you give us -- tell us what it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that these were problems within the then ruling and practically only party, the Serbian Democratic Party, and that it had to do with personal power within the party. I don't think it had anything particular to do with the events, apart from these internal reasons which I think were to a large degree personal. I think that one of the major issues was who were the persons who believed themselves those who were to be honoured because the corridor had been broken through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you say "I think." What specifically in relation to the editor-in-chief? What were the reasons? Do you know? If you don't know, if you say, I just think it was this or that. Did he claim anything? Were there others who said he had done things wrong? What was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that he claimed that, together with some other circles, he was to be most credited for having broken the corridor. But as far as I know, it was an operation of the Army of Republika Srpska, and this created political differences within the party. But I did not know the particulars because I never was a member of this party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you say, "I think that he claimed that, together with some other circles, he was to be most credited," why do you think that? What's your knowledge about what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of what was published in Glas these days, because they said that some paramilitaries had broken the corridor, and on the other hand -- I think that he was the one who was saying that, that it was the paramilitaries. And on the other hand, it was clear that it was a very widespread, major military operation. But the party circles are closed and therefore it was only the rumours that reached me from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And therefore whether the abolishment of the Crisis Staff were entirely foreign to that, you wouldn't know because you only heard rumours and you have no direct knowledge. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to clarify something, I will read to you what has been recorded in the transcript and you can then just check if it's correct. On page 44, line 21, it reads: [In English] "... I think he was the one who was saying that, that it was the paramilitaries."

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, he wasn't saying that. Some of the members of the SDS political party had this conviction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let us please look at P7193. You have seen this document also. It's the letter to Daniel Salvatore Schiffer sent by Dr. Radovan Karadzic. It reads that the Serbian side is willing to release all the prisoners from Manjaca if the international community and the ICRC are ready to accept them and convey them to third countries. Do you know what those who were imprisoned in Manjaca requested?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They requested to leave for third countries. I think that a large number of them left Banja Luka for London by air. I think that those were mostly wounded people and those who were in poor condition, because Daniel Schiffer came there then and the camp was closed in his presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the source of your information, that this is what the people in Manjaca requested?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably because they did go to London on a plane. It was a big Russian plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you did not personally talk about this with people in Manjaca -- or did you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I had no opportunity and I didn't really deal with these issues at the time. This was a very dynamic period when there was quite a lot of other work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now just look at another two documents. I think that we'll finish one of them before the break. P7194, please. In this document, we need page 4 in the English version and page 3 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a document in which some things have been crossed out. What is discussed here are the poor conditions in Omarska, the fact that sanitary and other equipment was inadequate, and that there were too many people. In the continuation of the same paragraph, we read this sentence: "However, we are forced to use them, one of the reasons being that the other side is not interested in the least in an exchange of prisoners." As you were working in the paper of the 1st Krajina Corps, did you have the information whether the other side was uninterested in an exchange of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. The paper wasn't being published at the time. We were just preparing it. The first issue under number 11 was only published in November.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll also need P7195.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we move to that, I'm addressing both you, Mr. Lukic, and you, Mr. Traldi. Of course we see that there are quite a lot of handwritings in it. Well, the witness commented on it, where -- but the Chamber would like to know, of course, what the status of this document is in the view of the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: What I can say is we got it from a media source rather than from a Republika Srpska government collection, which indicates to us that it was sent in this form. And the source was affiliated with SRNA.
