utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But do you know who then -- whether they received it with all the handwritten markings on it or did they make their own markings on it, the source that received this press release?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: That, Your Honour, I don't have an answer to. And we'll look into it and report back as expeditiously as we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I noticed that you quoted only from the parts which were not stricken out. Mr. Lukic, do you have any comment on the matter? Because earlier I think you did not object to the admission, but we still may need some --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I did not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- information in order to assess the exact probative value of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I did not because I saw some stamp on the first page that somebody received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And there is a signature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What's then your position in relation to this document, that the text was given to press agencies with the markings on it or without?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I really -- we have no knowledge who did those markings, whether it was done after it was sent or before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you -- because you're now putting questions in relation to this document, you accept this to be a press release with or without the markings which was once issued?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that situation is clear. Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see we are at the break time but I can finish in a couple of minutes so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please finish in those couple of minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So we need P7195, please. [Interpretation] It's a video.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were told that between the 5th and the 7th the barbed wire had been removed. The journalist Penny Marshall said on the 7th when she was filming this, the 7th of August, 1992, she says that the visit is strictly supervised. Did you see that? Could journalists freely speak to the people who were in Trnopolje or was somebody escorting them, some armed persons? What was your impression? Was it a strictly supervised visit?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the journalists freely spoke. At Trnopolje there were about 40 journalists. There was a bus full of them. There was an escort, but it wasn't there just for escort purposes. It was there for the security of the journalists. Can I just say a few words? Serbia and Republika Srpska were under UN sanctions and embargo then, and the attitude of the population towards anything that was called "foreign" was very negative, and I said that in my statement. Our main intention was to safe-guard the journalists so that nothing bad would happen to them. And I can say with pride that there was no threat to the physical security of journalists in our area. There were civilian cars that were driving in front of the bus and behind the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just another thing. As far as you know, now these posts where it is claimed that there was a barbed wire around them, what did this area look like when you were there on the 7th?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember a barbed wire. I remember this wire mesh. Any peasant puts barbed wire on top of a fence in our parts. It was old and it was rusty. I know that the entire area was not fenced off with barbed wire. There was this fencing there from earlier on. There was a school there or a youth centre, and usually there would be fences around that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How high was the fencing?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It varied. Mostly it was low and in some parts it was a bit higher, probably the part facing the forest. I mean, I don't know why. It was done a lot earlier. I never really gave this any thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say "lower," how much lower?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our fences are usually 1 metre, 1 metre, 20 centimetres. I mean, that's a tradition in our parts, that is what everybody does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there parts that were not fenced off at all?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were. More than a half, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Solaja. That was all we had for you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I may have one or two short questions. First of all: Now, finally, when you were there on the 7th of August, if I understand you well, was there any barbed wire anywhere that you did see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was there only once. And as far as I know, I didn't see it. I mean, a barbed wire fence? I did not see that. We have this tradition, and I also have it on my own property, that on top of a fence you put barbed wire. But I don't know whether your understanding is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Witness, I'm just seeking facts. Did you see, not in your own garden, but did you see any barbed wire when you were in Trnopolje on the 7th of August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you comment that the barbed wire was rusty. What is the basis of your knowledge that the barbed wire you didn't see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mesh. That is a fence that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If it's entered "barbed wire," we would ask to be revised [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that there is a misunderstanding in that respect. Yes. That's clear. I have one other question. I'm seeking clarification of paragraph 31 of your statement. Perhaps it could be -- or 30, 31, of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which is now D924.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I already introduced the matter to you. You told us that there were no camps in Banja Luka, which you explained was that wherever they may have been located, they were not organised by Banja Luka authorities. And then in paragraph 30, you further say about there was -- a terrible fact is that there were several cases of murder which were discussed only later. And you then later say that you know about a few murders. And then in paragraph 31, you said: "Even at that time, all of that was resolved and proven to be motivated by greed." Now, I am just trying to understand what murders you are talking about. The two murders you are referring to, I think, are not murders which appear in the indictment. In the indictment we have a number of incidents where sometimes a smaller number, sometimes a larger number of people were killed. Now, if you say -- if you are talking about these murders, are you talking about a limited area or are you including any of the murders which this Chamber finds in the indictment as charges against the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know of these two cases. This murder --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not understand the names that were mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I knew these persons myself and the crime prevention police said that these murders involved looting as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's for those two and not in general for murders having been committed at that period of time in the larger area in or close to Banja Luka, Prijedor, Sanski Most. You're not explaining any other murders than the two which you specifically mention here. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood that correctly. Those are the cases that I know about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Traldi, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. President. Five minutes or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll continue for five minutes. Please proceed. Further Cross-examination by Mr. Traldi:

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First, sir, you mentioned prisoners at Manjaca who you said went by plane to the United Kingdom. Now, the prisoners, when Manjaca was closed, more than a thousand were sent to Croatia by bus and several hundred were transferred to Batkovic and Kula within the Bosnian Serb system and hidden from the Red Cross; weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about this convoy to Croatia, but I don't know about -- about other camps. And I don't think it's realistic, because the Red Cross had very precise records. Beat Schweizer is a person I knew myself from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you are not asked about an opinion, how realistic is anything. We do understand that you do know about the transport to Croatia and that you do not know about the transfer of others. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understood that well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Finally, could we have 65 ter 02362.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And I'm calling this up -- this will be the transcript of the 22nd Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly related to your comments on redirect about the civil nature of the Bosnian Serb state and the reference to Serbs as well as other peoples in the constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we could have page 77 at the bottom in English and 75 at the bottom in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And we see at the end of what are described as the chairman's remarks that the assembly is moving to item 10 of the agenda, that's a citizenship bill, and that someone named Mr. Milojevic speaks. He describes here in the English the great importance of that bill for the state. And then if we turn to the next page in the English, we read Milojevic say, describing his concerns about the bill, it says: "First, contravention with the Constitution. Article 1 of the Constitution stipulates: 'Republika Srpska is the state of the Serbian people.' Period." Now, first, were you aware of that position, that Republika Srpska was the state of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one MP speaking and I cannot identify with that. This is his personal position, and it is the assembly that formulates general positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And is it your position that the constitution of Republika Srpska did not stipulate that it was the state of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify that question? I did not understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sure. What I'm putting to you is he's not articulating a personal position. He's saying Article 1 of the constitution stipulates Republika Srpska is the state of the Serbian people. He's purporting to be quoting the constitution. You are aware of that provision as well; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given what I've said already, namely, and other citizens, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And he adds: "Citizens of Republika Srpska shall be granted citizenship of Republika Srpska, which means everybody, and he says, 'I think it should read Serbian.'"

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: If we turn to the next page -- sorry, if we turn back in the English and to the next page in the B/C/S. I was imprecise and I apologise. We see at the end of the third paragraph in the B/C/S or in the third paragraph that he is discussing how Serbs couldn't get citizenship in Slovenia straight away. In Croatia, the parliament, the assembly decides which Muslim will get citizenship. And then he moves that the law be sent back. And if we turn -- below that we see Mr. Krajisnik's remarks and in pertinent part in the middle, he says: "That's why we decided that citizenship should be Serbian since our republic is Serbian." Below that, we see Mr. Milijanovic, he says: "I think we need to make an effort to make this law as short and clear as possible." Turning to the next page in the English. And at the very bottom in the B/C/S, we see the chairman say: "Mr. Milijanovic's objection and proposal are valid." And turning to the next page in the B/C/S, the law is being sent back to the relevant ministry for improvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So the truth is that the constitution referred to Republika Srpska as the state of Serbian people in Article 1 and that the citizenship policy was designed to promote Serb citizenship, that, as Mr. Krajisnik said, citizenship should be Serbian because the republic is Serbian; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can now present my own position, if necessary. This is the parliamentary debate that I am unaware of. And it's very early, the 23rd, the 24th of April, 1992. From this one can see that this article about Serbs and other citizens did exist and that it was a subject of debate. So I maintain my position that the constitution reflects the position that it is the country of Serbs and other citizens, and after all this is contained in any modern constitution. I think the parliamentary debates cannot lead me to the conclusion of the assembly, and I would kindly ask to be shown that so that I could see what it was. This is just a parliamentary debate and ultimately it leads to certain decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, here we've showed you that it led to the bill being sent back. I'm going to ask you just one final question, which is: Saying Serbs and others, obviously by only mentioning Serbs it gives Serbs primacy, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS SOLAJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd ask that this assembly session be marked for identification. We'll seek to agree a selection with the Defence. Similarly, because it's discussed just in this assembly session and also in the witness's answer on redirect, I admit I haven't checked on the status of the constitution but we'll check Article 1 as well to ensure that the official wording is before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. In view of this last comment, I would invite the witness to briefly explain why you do not agree with Mr. Traldi that Serbs are given primacy in the text as it was quoted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it is the way the preamble to the constitutional provision says; namely that, at least according to the constitution, all citizens enjoy equal rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number for this portion of the transcript of the assembly session would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be P7196.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Marked for identification. This then concludes your testimony, Mr. Solaja. Mr. Solaja, I would like to thank you very much for having come a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRALDI
utterances.text: Just to ensure there isn't anything sitting on the record unaddressed, I have done a quick check. The constitution is P3007 and so we won't be seeking to do anything further in that regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We take a break. We will resume at 25 minutes to 2.00 -- to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to briefly address some - I'm not saying all - of the scheduling issues raised recently, that is. But the first one, and I would say the most urgent one, is the one for the week after Orthodox Easter, which is the week, Mr. Lukic, of the -- starting on Monday, the 13th of April. The Chamber has seriously considered to see whether we could use that Thursday and Friday in one way or another, and similar suggestions were made by the -- by the Prosecution. We have decided that we'll grant the whole of that week as a non-sitting week, and I immediately add to that not as a nonworking week, because one of the reasons was that we anticipated on what we still -- what you announced, that is, that you would ask for some extra time for the preparation of the reopening of the Defence case -- of the Prosecution's case. Now in view of that, and not having yet seen your submissions in that respect, but already those two days we were considering -- oh, yes, well, but even the two weeks we had still in the back of our mind as possibly using. We refrain from that. But then again, this time of non-sitting also means that you have additional time to prepare for whatever comes after that week. And whether that will be -- whether that will be extended in any other way, we'll first wait for any submissions to be made in that respect. All the other scheduling issues about the week of the -- starting the 26th of May, I think we have dealt with that one already. That is a non-sitting week as well, although an extra Friday will be used in the first week of June. That remains unchanged. I leave it to that at this moment. Is the Defence ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We are, Your Honours. The Defence would call Mr. Bojan Subotic at this time, no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Subotic. Before you give --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make the solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Subotic. Mr. Subotic, it usually stays better if you have it on the top of your head. Mr. Subotic, it will be Mr. Ivetic, and you find him to your left, who will examine you. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir. Could you please state your full name so that it is properly entered into the record.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: My name is Bojan Subotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did you have occasion to give a written statement to members of the Defence team of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up 1D01645 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you could look on the screen at the Serbian original and tell us whose signature that is on the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: My signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, I note that the year of birth is different between the Serbian original and the English translation. Can you please verify for us what is your correct date and year of birth?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: The exact date of my birth is the 12th of December, 1972. It's the version in Serbian. And the other one is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could now turn to the last page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: There is a signature here. Can you tell us whose signature appears on this page?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: That is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, does the date which is recorded here correspond to your recollection of the date when you would have signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. Yes, yes. It was the month of June. Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, after you signed this statement, did you have an opportunity to review the same and read it in full to ascertain if everything is accurately and correctly recorded therein?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I had the opportunity to look at it fleetingly. There were some -- whether those were typos or something was moved, some of the events which may have occurred earlier or later in the written statement. But all in all, everything's in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me go through some of those typos with you. If I'd look at the first -- pardon me, the second page in both languages, and paragraph number 1, I note that the English translation again has the wrong year of birth. Should that be fixed to reflect 1972 as we previously mentioned and as is in the Serbian original?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The one uploaded says 1972, isn't it? Well, let me just have a look. Oh, you -- no, no, you're right. I made a mistake. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we could look at the third page in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In regard to paragraphs 11 and 12, what order should these paragraphs go in to correctly correspond to the chronology of the events contained therein?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that paragraphs 11 and 12 should switch places. So paragraph 11 should be in the place of paragraph 12, and the other way around. According to what I remember and the statement that I gave, this should be the right chronology. Whether this was switched so that it stands as it is now while the document was typed or something else, I'm not sure. Because I talk here about meeting with my commander, so it should be switched. Paragraph 12 should be in place of paragraph 11 and vice versa.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, apart from these corrections, do you stand by the rest of the statement as written?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. What I see on the screen, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, if I were to ask you questions today in court based on the same matters as contained in your written statement, would your answers to those questions today in court be substantially the same as already written in your statement?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you have taken a solemn declaration today to tell the truth. Does that mean that what is written in your statement is truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time we would tender 1D01645 as the next public Defence exhibit. There are no associated documents with the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. HASAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the number would be D926.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D926 is admitted into evidence. I nevertheless, Mr. Ivetic, would like to briefly deal with the -- you said the chronology as found in paragraphs 11 and 12. Witness, you say we should -- as a matter of fact, 12 comes before 11. Now, in 11, you were given instructions to patrol the area along a stretch, et cetera, et cetera. And then in 12, it starts with: "During the patrol, I was under fire all the time ..." If we change the chronology and start with 12, then the order for a patrol was given after you had patrolled that stretch, which is not entirely clear to me. Do you have any clarification as to how you can talk about a patrol which is only later ordered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I meant only with regard to the instructions which my commander issued to me. Paragraph 11 says that he was there then. However, no, a soldier reported to me then that he had called, that he had told me to stay there, to replenish my ammunition, and continue patrolling. So I was on patrol before that and under heavy fire. So before I had reached this soldier and my commander, and that's what is now contained in paragraph 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the soldier which reported to you that he had called -- that he had told you to stay there to replenish your ammunition, does that appear at this moment somewhere in paragraphs 11 and 12? If you could just read it again. It's on your screen, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraphs 11 and 12 do not mention the soldier. The soldier I'm talking about is a soldier who was at the reception of the facility to which I withdrew when I managed to get out of the ambush I had been in together with my soldiers. In other words, my intention was to withdraw, to pick up this soldier, and to withdraw towards Milici because I was attacked by a huge force. However, this soldier informed me that my commander, Malinic, had told him that I shouldn't budge and that he would be arriving there, too, very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But in 12, I also read that you took a group of 10 to 15 Muslim soldiers and that you went with them to the battalion command. Now, what did you do? Did you withdraw or did you bring imprisoned soldiers or at least soldiers that had surrendered and were disarmed to the battalion command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in paragraph 11, when this soldier informed me about that, I replenished my ammunition and I heard down in the area of Nova Kasaba, the stadium, towards Konjevic Polje, there was heavy fire. I then went in an armoured combat vehicle with my five soldiers and I was ambushed down there, so I was hit with -- I don't know with what exactly anymore. But my armoured combat vehicle could no longer be used. And during this ambush, the exchange between me and the Muslim soldiers, those 13 or 14 soldiers surrendered themselves to me. I don't know what the exact number was. I did not take them up to the barracks or the school, but I called a first class sergeant, whose name I cannot remember, to come and get them. I also had a wounded soldier there, so I asked them to call for an ambulance for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it's therefore not just changing the chronology but also quite some additional information. Let me just check whether the ambulance was -- did you state anywhere in 11, 12 that you were injured and that an ambulance was called? I don't see any of that in 11 and 12.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it wasn't me who was wounded but one of my soldiers. And I called this first class sergeant who was up there to come down here to take over the prisoners and at the same time if he could communicate to the medical service in Milici -- it's true I did not mention that in my statement, but I did have a wounded soldier and I asked for medical assistance for him. However, it did not reach me. I transported this wounded soldier and delivered him to this first class sergeant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And when did you then talk to the soldiers that had surrendered? You didn't accompany them to the battalion command. When did you then talk to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I talked to them there on the spot where they had surrendered themselves to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I'm just trying to understand the change in chronology as you testified about. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I need to read the witness summary at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Bojan Subotic became a member of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment of the VRS in December of 1992 and served in various posts including the posts of commander of the anti-terrorist platoon and military police. He recalls in the first half of July 1995, when on regular duty at the command of the Military Police Battalion at Nova Kasaba, a woman came to them to say that her house and the area around the house was full of Muslim soldiers. He went to check with one other soldier, and they came under ambush and fire from the Muslims, and had to call a BOV armoured vehicle to withdraw. In his estimate, there were 1.000 enemy soldiers with dozens of machine-guns. Hearing intense fire from machine-gun and mortars in the direction of Konjevic Polje, he set out in the BOV to that area because there were a lot of civilians there. His vehicle came under fire and he fired tear-gas into the woods. Muslim soldiers surrendered to him and told of how there was infighting on their side between those that had wanted to surrender and the Muslim commanders who did not let them surrender and who were killing those that wanted to give themselves up. He used the vehicle's loudspeaker to call upon the Muslims to surrender and additional Muslims surrendered. Three of the surrendered Muslims were wounded and were bandaged up. Subotic radioed the command and asked for an ambulance and assistance so as not to be wiped out as there were still movements and shooting from the Muslim troops in the woods. At the base, even the UNPROFOR were firing into the woods to repel the attack. The witness eventually went into the woods with the Muslims and saw a horrible sight of over 500 dead people. They removed some wounded that they found. All the surrendered and wounded were at the Nova Kasaba football stadium. He went and brought 100 to 150 loaves of bread to distribute to them and all the food the base had. At one point General Mladic came and spoke to the men, receiving an applause from the Muslims. He told them that everyone would be housed and fed and exchanged for Serb prisoners. He ordered that they be secured and safely transported in buses to Bratunac where the civilian authorities would take them over. The witness escorted a column of buses containing these Muslims to the Vuk Karadzic school in Bratunac where he turned them over to civilian police. And that completes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further questions for the witness, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 2 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to look at paragraph 6 with you. And, Mr. Subotic, I'd like to ask you first to tell us about this woman that came to you and said her house was full of Muslims. Was she someone known to you from before?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes, I knew her.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What was her ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I think that she was a Serb. Yes, she was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And where was her house located?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, her house was looking from our command to the west, perhaps 2- or 300 metres from the seat of our command; that is to say, this school.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what did she tell you about how it is that she had noted the presence of Muslims troops in and around her house?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I was then at the reception of our facility, our command. It was perhaps around 7.00, 7.30 a.m., immediately after breakfast. She came running to us, barefoot and out of her wits. We saw her running towards us and we thought that something had happened to her, to her children, because there had been several incidents with the neighbours. Sometimes we would provide medical assistance to children during the night if they had high fever or something like that, and that's what I had in mind. However, when she came to us, she said, "Look, you are sitting here and having fun and my house is full of Turks," she emphasized, but she meant the Muslims. That was how I understood her. And she also added that her children had remained in the house. She told it not only to me but to all of us who were there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 7 you describe that you were ambushed while going towards the house. Could you tell us about this ambush and precisely what happened?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: I'm not receiving interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's try it again. In paragraph 7, sir, you talk about being ambushed while going towards the house. Can you tell us about this ambush and precisely what happened?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: So when she came and stated that her house was full of Muslims, I was in the reception room. I took one soldier with me to go in reconnaissance to check the truthfulness of her story, and I ordered two other soldiers to be in the armoured combat vehicle and to be at the ready and to turn on the ignition, because that's one of the rules of the manner in which military police is supposed to work. So I when I set out towards her house, it's about 200 metres, and there is a river there called Jadar, and there is a bend in the river. While crossing it, I really saw many soldiers. I didn't know whose soldiers they were, I couldn't see their insignia, but those soldiers fired at me. It was heavy machine-gun fire. Even a mortar, 60-millimetre, the small infantry mortar, also fired at me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now in paragraph 8 you state that you could see about 1.000 Muslim soldiers there, and you estimate they had dozens of machine-guns. First of all, explain to us how it was you were able to see and observe all this?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, when they were firing at me, I responded using my own fire and my soldier, who had a machine-gun then, did too, but we didn't have a lot of ammunition. The clearing between the river and the house is about 150 metres, and I just happened to have binoculars there, and it was always there. And then in terms of her statement that there were people in the woods, I took the binoculars, and then during this short pause, when I started firing at them, they didn't stop firing. However, they were withdrawing towards the woods. So they weren't moving towards me. They were really getting out of her house, as she had said that they were inside, and they started withdrawing towards the woods. I looked through the binoculars, say, for 15 or 20 seconds, for instance, and I saw that there were almost 1.000 men. I wouldn't know what the exact number would be. I went to football games, I went to stadiums, but I cannot tell exactly. About a thousand. I counted about 30, 40 machine-guns, and I can tell the difference between an ordinary automatic rifle and a machine-gun. So some could be heard from the other side. And my opinion to this day is that they did have about 50 machine-guns in this group of 1.000 men. Well, that's not really a group. In my mind it's a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did they have any other armaments apart from these 30 to 40 machine-guns that you have identified?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, classical infantry weapons. These rifles, automatic, semi-automatic. They had a hand grenades and some of them had rifle grenades in their pockets, like we used to do as well. So they had it in their pockets of their flak jackets as well. We did that too so that we would be prepared to act. I think that these are rifle grenades. I don't think that it's a heavier weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn to page 3 in both languages, and paragraphs 10 and 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you now tell us how and when you were able to contact Major Malinic and when he actually arrived at the location?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Major Malinic, my battalion commander, he was there all the time. However, at that moment, when that woman came to see us and when there was this ambush, when I got caught in that ambush, he wasn't there. I think he was in Milici - it's a town, 7 to 10 kilometres away from Nova Kasaba - along with two other officers who arrived the day before that I think for some training. They went for breakfast. And when I got out, that is to say, when I asked for BOV to come and get me out, that is to say, from this armoured vehicle, there was fire aimed at enemy soldiers so they were acting as my support. I and this soldier who went with me were withdrawing, and I was thinking that day, that moment, that I should take the soldier who was at the gate, the two Dutch soldiers that were down there at the school -- and I don't know exactly -- now, there were a few cooks, I think, and a few soldiers, and then to withdraw towards the town of Milici because I saw that I was being attacked by a force that should be reckoned with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I went to the gate to carry this out, the soldier who was at the gate told me that he had received a telephone call from Major Malinic, and he said that I should get more ammunition and wait for him there, which is what I did. However, while getting the ammunition for the armoured vehicle and for us, because we had two combat kits there, we didn't have more than that for securing the school, I heard strong mortar fire, machine-gun fire, fighting in general in the area of Konjevic Polje and the Nova Kasaba stadium. I was thinking and I realised that civilians were living there, including children and the elderly. I set out with four of my soldiers and this combat vehicle, went down there. I told the soldier at the reception desk where I was going and that he should inform me via radio communication when Major Malinic arrives.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what happened to you and the combat vehicle when you set off for the area of Konjevic Polje and the Nova Kasaba stadium?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, immediately after crossing the bridge in Nova Kasaba, I was hit from the direction of the forest; that is to say, machine-gun fire was opened at me. But I was hit by some kind of anti-armour weapon. I had a wounded soldier there and my vehicle was also attacked, and it wasn't destroyed altogether. It was just the tires that were gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, now in relation to the events in paragraph 12, where you talk about six tear-gas canisters being fired into the woods, when did these events occur that we now talked about when your tires were shot out and your BOV came under fire? When did that occur in relation to the events in paragraph 12?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, it happened just then, when I was hit at that bridge. I ordered the soldiers to get out of the combat vehicle so that it would not be hit again. But again, I gave orders to the driver because he was the one who was supposed to handle that, so he fired these canisters, as these canisters are part of the equipment of such a combat vehicle. It's tear-gas that is used against riots and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, sir, could you speak more slowly so that the interpreters can get every word that you say. Now, you started telling us where you got the tear-gas from, I believe, and you said that these canisters are part of the equipment of such a combat vehicle. Could you please continue your answer from that point on.

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: It's not "kanistri" in Serbian. It's 40 millilitres, canisters of 40 millilitres that is part of the equipment for a military vehicle, and it's used for the military police and it's used for preventing riots. So it is not lethal but they can harm a human being.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us precisely about why you made the decision to fire the tear-gas? What was the reasons behind it?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I made this decision for two reasons. One reason is that I did not have any kind of heavy weapons to defend myself and to get out of there except for this machine-gun that is mounted on the vehicle and our rifles. Secondly, this tear-gas does affect personnel and at the same time there would be a smoke-screen, so I could cover myself in that way because I saw that there was no other way of handling the situation but trying to withdraw, to get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now how long did this whole situation last before you were able to get back to the base at the school?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, from the moment when I left the base, the school, and including that wounding of my soldier, and this ambush, and the firing of tear-gas -- well, I don't know. An hour and a half, two hours, that's how long it took from the first ambush. Something like that. I cannot say exactly now. I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now in relation to the events that are described in paragraph 11, where do these events that we've just talked about - the firing of the tear-gas and the hour and a half, two hours that transpired - where do they place chronologically in relation to what is described in paragraph 11, the contact with Major Malinic?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, that woman came to the gate about 7.30, and I first got in touch with Major Malinic after these first 15 Muslim soldiers were taken prisoner; that is to say, it was about two hours, something like that, so about 10.00, 10.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look now at paragraph -- well, first of all, can you tell us how it came to pass that the first 10 to 15 Muslim soldiers surrendered to you?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: When I fired the tear-gas towards the forest, enemy fire abated, almost stopped, because they were confused by the tear-gas. They probably didn't have gas masks and other protective gear. Since I got out of the shelter to see the extent of the damage done to the vehicle and also I and this soldier of my wanted to help our wounded soldier who was hit by a bullet in the neck. So this group that was not in front of us but from the Jadar River valley underneath the bridge, they came from under the bridge with their hands up. They surrendered to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And now if you look at paragraph 13, you talk of speaking to these 10 to 15 soldiers and of using the loudspeaker on the command vehicle to call on other Muslims to surrender. When did this happen, that is to say, in relation to the time-frame when your BOV was struck and you fired the tear-gas canisters? How soon after did you use the loudspeaker the first time to call for Muslims to surrender?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, when they surrendered to me, I ordered them to put down their weapons, which is what they had started doing even before I issued that order. They walked up to me to where the combat vehicle was, and it's only then that I saw that these were Muslim soldiers, because I saw the insignia on their sleeves. In the morning I didn't even know who it was that had fired at me. During that morning fighting -- well, the UNPROFOR forces -- I mean, the two of them, one of them fired into the woods because we really didn't know who was attacking us. When we talked to them after the surrender, all of that took about half an hour, 15 minutes, what they explained to me was that actually we were attacked by the entire 28th Division, the Srebrenica Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at what point in time did you use the loudspeaker on the combat vehicle? Was it at that time or sometime later; that is to say, before or after you had had contact with Major Malinic, yourself personally?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, immediately then I used the loudspeaker because the Muslim soldiers persuaded me to do that. What they said to me was that there were some other people up there in the hills that wanted to surrender. They even gave me names, names and surnames of these people. And then I remembered that I had that loudspeaker so that I could reach out to them. And the first thing that I said, that they shouldn't fire at us anymore from up there, that I had some of their men there, and then I started using some of these names that they had given me. Now, were they family members? Were they their comrades? I don't know. So it was already then that I started using the loudspeaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we look at paragraph 16 of the statement - and we need to go to page 4 in the Serbian for that - sir, did these Muslim soldiers telling you about their commanders that were killing people who wanted to surrender, did they give any details as to the identity of the commanders that were doing that on their side?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, that first group, no. But the second group that surrendered to me, they said their komandirs, and they mentioned a name like Tursunovic, he was their boss, their commander, whatever, they kept complaining about him all the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I seek clarification. A little bit earlier you talked about the UNPROFOR forces, and then you said: "... I mean, the two of them, one of them fired into the woods because we really didn't know who was attacking us." These UNPROFOR soldiers, where were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were with us at the battalion command, in that facility where I was staying, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they stayed in the command or did they leave the command at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They spent that entire day at the command. They opened fire. When I withdrew, while I was getting more ammunition, while the first attack was still going on, one of them -- actually, that morning, we were all having coffee together at the reception desk. And when they started firing at us from the forest, then I went towards the river, I managed to get back, and as I was getting more ammunition and as I alerted the unit, the entire facility was under fire. One of these soldiers asked that I give him a weapon. I gave him my very own rifle. He was in a trench together with my soldier at the gate, and they opened fire together because we didn't know who was firing at us. But at any rate, we were under fire. It was coming from the forest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But they stayed in the command. They never were in any vehicle together with you or one of your men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. They stayed at the command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why were they there? It's still -- UNPROFOR suddenly in the middle of your command. I'm just wondering what were they doing there having breakfast with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They came to us a day before that and they asked us for help. They had problems with some of our -- well, paramilitary units. That's what they said. They were, I think, taking weapons, vehicles, whatever. I have no idea. So they came to see us. The day before all of this happened they were received there, they asked us for help so that we could protect them and their equipment, their weapons and so on. Two vehicles arrived. However, during the night, one vehicle left with two or three soldiers and yet another vehicle with these two soldiers spent the night there at the base. They were with us, played cards with us, had meals with us, and so on. I really don't know what their intention was, but they were asking the military police for help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And did they come with their own vehicle, a UN vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And they used that or was that vehicle used at any point in time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That vehicle was parked next to our vehicles, and their weapons were locked in their vehicle. They had the key, and I know - I remember full well - that one of them wanted to go to the vehicle to get weapons. However, the gun-fire was so strong that he certainly would have been killed, and that's why he asked me for a weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I say "whether the vehicle was used," I mean was it driven anywhere by anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was parked, the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it stayed there, as far as you're aware of, all the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it stayed there after them too, because I personally saw them off, the two of them. They did not feel safe in that vehicle because it was not armoured. They asked for our armoured vehicle, so I personally saw them off to the base in Potocari. They left us their vehicle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Voluntarily. They gave it as a present to you or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, not as a present. My commander, Major Malinic, issued some kind of receipt to them and that's how they left that vehicle at our base. Was it a receipt or what kind of document it was, I really don't know, but I know it was some kind of document because they didn't want to take that vehicle because that road, Nova Kasaba-Konjevic Polje-Potocari, was under fire. And my understanding was that they did not feel safe in their vehicle and that's why they asked for an armoured vehicle to take them to Potocari. And they asked for our escort, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was just putting these questions because suddenly the UNPROFOR soldiers became part of your testimony, where I didn't know exactly how to understand that. Mr. Ivetic, please -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One short clarification I would like to ask the witness for. You mentioned the second group of Muslim soldiers who surrendered to you and your unit, and you said they mentioned a name like, something, who was their boss or their commander. Can you repeat the name of that commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding was then that they were mentioning Tursunovic, they called him Tursun, but it was Tursunovic. He was some kind of chief commander of theirs. I don't know the exact name but they did mention the name of Tursunovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now just to finish off with the UNPROFOR, since we have started that topic, on page 7 in both languages of the statement and paragraph 39 of the same, you talk of escorting the UNPROFOR members to their base in Potocari. First of all, who asked you to escort and deliver these persons to Potocari?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Major Malinic, my commander, issued that order to me that morning, that I prepare a patrol, an armoured combat vehicle, BOV, and to carry out this task; that is to say, to escort two members of UNPROFOR back to their base in Potocari. Who gave him this order and who asked him to do that, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And to whom did you hand over the UNPROFOR personnel when you arrived at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't hand them over to anyone. We arrived at their base and there was a soldier there, I don't know what he was exactly. He had a uniform on and a big moustache. They said goodbye to us and they said "hvala" in Serbian, they thanked us, and they stayed at their base in Potocari and we went back to our base.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now if we could go back to page 4 in both languages and paragraph 22 of your statement. You talk about -- you talk about giving the Muslims who were at the stadium what food you had in the barracks and getting some bread from shops, 100 to 150 loaves of bread. Did you have any consequences from this activity of bringing bread from these shops?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Several groups surrendered to me on that day. It was water that was the biggest problem of all, because the heat was unbearable that day. I have never experienced heat like that in my life. And the second problem was food. We had bread and we had rations for about 48 hours, so we shared that with them. And I was given an order by Major Malinic to go to Milici, and on the basis of my official ID of a military policemen, I was authorised to take bread from bakeries. On that day I went to Milici, I came back in about 15 to 20 minutes, it was already 12.00, 1.00, there wasn't a lot of bread because usually most of the bread is there in the morning. I got 150 to 200 loaves and I gave it to the POWs, and they shared it amongst themselves. Now, I don't know exactly, but two or three years after that, I was asked by the office of the prosecutor of the town of Vlasenica to come in, and there was a criminal report filed against me. I stood accused of taking bread from the owners of these bakeries because my army had probably not refunded that bread and I could not issue receipts. On that day I didn't have any such thing, but I used my military ID, including the number, so it was my personal ID. I went to the prosecutor's office in Vlasenica, I said all of that, and to this day nobody's called me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the usher please assist the witness in adjusting the earphones. They are not sitting at the right place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn to paragraph 23, which will be on the next page in the Serbian original.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here, sir, you describe that the only problem that you had with relation to the Muslims at Nova Kasaba stadium was some civilians of Serbian ethnicity who came to the stadium and protested. Can you tell us what these Serb civilians were doing precisely?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, they lived there in the area of Kasaba. There were about 50 of them there. About 50. As for military-age men, there were about 10 or 15 of them, and there were children, old men, women there. So we did have a problem. When we were taking these Muslim soldiers prisoner, we had a problem with them. At first they threw stones at them, bricks, whatever it was that they found on the road. And after that, we had to line up, and I really felt like tear-gassing these people who were casting these objects. Also, they were issuing threats, they were swearing, and so on, but we couldn't stop that. At any rate, they didn't manage to touch them and they stopped throwing stones at them and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, for --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're at the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, for very practical purposes, we do understand that you would need 50 to 60 minutes. Now, if it would be 60 minutes, then that would be another 20 minutes from now. Then, of course, you could consider to go on until five minutes to 2.00 and then have the 20-minute break, but of course that would then bring us to the end of the day. If, however, it would be ten minutes, then we would still have to start the cross-examination. I'm a bit uncertain as well about how much time you would still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have about 18 minutes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, I have 38 recorded -- oh, 18 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 18 to 20 minutes. That's -- according to my questions, that's what I should have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. 18 to 20 minutes left. Then you could -- if -- but please consult with Mr. Mladic, we could continue for another 18 minutes and then adjourn for the day, or we could now take the break and then have the last 20 minutes after that. I leave it in your hands what you'd prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I've been authorised to keep going, so that's what I'll do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we'll conclude the examination-in-chief today and have an early adjournment. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to turn to paragraphs 18 and 19 with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have to go back one page in the Serbian, I think. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And here you talk about when you went into the woods and viewed the horrible sight of 500 dead soldiers. First of all, can you describe the geographic layout of the land where these bodies were located?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, it's an area 3- or 400 metres away from the main road, Nova Kasaba-Konjevic Polje road. I think that today it's called Jela village, but I'm not sure. To the right there are streams. The terrain is awful. It's not level. There are those streams or brooks, there is woods, there is thicket. While going up for about 200 metres, you reach a meadow. When you cross the meadow, to the right in a copse, there is a big brook and that is where I stepped on the first bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now in relation to what you said earlier in your statement about hearing intense fire from various directions, was one of the directions where you previously heard fire exchanges coming from this area?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, that was the direction from which I heard a lot of firing in the morning, and it wasn't clear to me what was going on. I was the leader of the patrol that day and I patrolled along that stretch, and I knew that there was no strong military unit from our side there. So it wasn't clear to me where that fire was coming from. And later on this was confirmed by everything that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you describe the dispersion of the bodies; that is to say, were they all in one place? Or if not, how wide of an area are we talking about where these approximately 500 bodies were seen by you?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, they were not in one single occasion. They were in a radius of perhaps 3- to 4- or 500 metres. I don't know exactly. I cannot remember. In several spots. Somewhere there were 2 bodies, some were 10, some there were 50. What I saw were irregularly shaped wounds as if they were caused by shells or fragmentation mines, as if they had come on them, or as if someone threw grenades on them. There were few people who had been shot from infantry weapons. So they lay in several locations in this radius of 3- or 400 metres. I was going there with the two Muslim prisoners because I wasn't even aware of this precise spot. It was they who had taken me there. And by doing that, I had violated the code of a military police because I shouldn't have left the armoured vehicle and the patrol. But when someone says 200 people, there is no reason not to believe them.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And did you have any indication how long these bodies had been there?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a hot day and already you could feel the unpleasant smell. It may have been during the night or during the morning. In some places, I saw blood that had already coagulated and in other places it was still flowing. So it may have been 6, 7, 8, or 10 hours. I am not a specialist, I'm not an expert, I'm not a pathologist. But during the night and in the morning it must have been that they had sustained these injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now on your back from this location, did anything happen to you?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: We found there five or six survivors, their soldiers who had been wounded but were still alive. We bandaged them. I told the two prisoners who had brought me there to take two of those who were lighter and carry them, and I with my men took another one. We left two behind. Later we sent people for them. My combat armoured vehicle called me by radio to tell me that a group of 200 men had surrendered themselves to them, and I ordered them to escort them to the stadium, and I would take a shortcut to reach the stadium. However, while we were carrying these people, Muslim soldiers took me prisoner. There must have been at least ten addressed me, behind them there were another 200, and they had come from the meadow that I had described. They told me to drop my gun, which I of course did. At that moment, one of the prisoners I had sent to carry the wounded men returned and he told them that I was helping them. I said that there were many people who had surrendered themselves and that if they wanted to do so too, that they should follow me. I asked if I could take my weapon and that they could follow me if they wanted, which they did. To this day, it's not really clear to me how come that it all happened as it did, but the people followed me and reached the stadium in Nova Kasaba. They threw down their weapons right there and then. We did not have sufficient forces to disarm them and to secure them and us, as we were supposed to do by the rules of the military police, but we had good co-operation with them with regard to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you about the time-period when General Mladic came to the Nova Kasaba stadium, which starts at page 5 in English, page 6 in Serbian, and starts at paragraph 29 of your statement. First of all, sir, were you present for the entirety of General Mladic's visit and stay at this location on that day?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just at the moment when General Mladic arrived to us at the stadium, I was coming downhill with some prisoners who had surrendered. Throughout his stay, I didn't go back. So all this time I was perhaps 3 or 4 metres away from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And during the time-period that General Mladic was present at Nova Kasaba stadium and when you were 3 to 4 metres from him, did you ever see or hear of anyone being killed at that location at the Nova Kasaba stadium in the presence of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: No, no, not at all. As long as General Mladic was there, but even otherwise, I'm not aware of anyone having been killed. There was one murder but it was a woman who killed a prisoner from a hunting rifle, but that was in the morning. I forgot to say that earlier. When I was ambushed at the bridge, a woman came with a hunting rifle and said that she had killed a Muslim who had entered her house. But I'm not aware of anyone having meddled with our prisoners who were secured by the military police. We did not even allow our civilians to approach our prisoners. We were doing it as professionally as we could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, just seeking one clarification. You said when you were ambushed, a woman came with a hunting rifle. That was not the same woman as the woman who reported -- who had reported that there were so many Muslims in and around her house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. Not the same woman. I knew the other woman, too. I think that Pogaca or something like that was her last name. She also lived close by the school but it wasn't the same woman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 30, you talk of General Mladic's order to secure the transfer of prisoners to the civilian authorities via bus. Did General Mladic give any additional orders as to how these prisoners should be treated?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, on General Mladic's arrival, to tell the truth, my commander and I didn't think that this was right because we couldn't provide adequate security for him. He somehow suddenly went in among them. He shook hands with some of them. Whether he had known them or whether he introduced himself, I didn't know. He talked with them about Alija, about the war, and they stood up and applauded. And he told them that they would be exchanged, that they should listen to us, the military policemen, that is to say, and he told us and told us strictly to take care of the prisoners, that some buses would be arriving within an hour, that the men should sign their names and that they would should all board the bus and deliver it to the civilian police in Bratunac. That is what I heard and saw then when General Mladic was present there at the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, in the course of all the activities that you've discussed, the various attacks and ambushes, during the course of that day, did you at that time have information about the VRS operation against the town of Srebrenica and its results?

utterances.speaker: BOJAN SUBOTIC
utterances.text: Well, no, I didn't have any information. I don't think that even my commander, Major Malinic, had any, because probably he wouldn't have left me alone with five men down there to secure a school. I was a young officer at the time, a sergeant. I was a tactician, not a strategist. So I really didn't have any information about any of that going on. The first thing I learned, personally, was when I took these five [as interpreted] men prisoner, and then they actually told me that the whole division had come upon me.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, the transcript records you as saying "these five men," is that in fact what you said, these five prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you for answering my questions on behalf of myself and my client, General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have one short question with respect to paragraph 31. In paragraph 31 -- and perhaps we could move to the next page in English. At the end you say: "I climbed on the vehicle and through the loudspeaker I told the Muslims in the field that they should come in an orderly fashion to -- and enter the buses." And then you say in your statement they should all board them in an orderly fashion and find are a place for themselves and before they get on the buses they should drink some water. Where was the water they could get?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There in Nova Kasaba at the football pitch where we were then. After General Mladic's order to take care of the prisoners, he turned personally to me, and said, "Kid, make sure that each prisoner should arrive to Bratunac," which I made sure later. And they drank the water. There was this river called Jadar, 50 to 70 metres next to the stadium. We let them go there to drink water and cool themselves because the day was really extremely hot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for the day, Mr. Subotic. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. But before you leave the courtroom, I would like to instruct you that you should not speak --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We have videolinks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, we have videolinks. I was just about to -- as a matter of fact, I was just about to address the videolinks. We'll not continue with your testimony tomorrow because videolinks have been scheduled. And I instruct you that whenever we will resume, and you will be kept updated by the Victims and Witness Section on when we expect to resume, but that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that is testimony you have given today or whether that is testimony still to be given in the near future. If you have understood this, then you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you are right because -- it must be that it's Monday morning, but the next brief item that I would like to address is the following: That you have scheduled or the Defence has scheduled a number of witnesses who will give their testimony via video-conference link this week, and everyone is aware that it takes quite some preparations, significant amount of time, effort, and resources to make these videolinks possible. We would like to hear from both parties whether they believe that the witness schedule for this week will be met. If the current schedule is not feasible, the Chamber would like to hear alternative proposals from the parties to ensure that the testimonies of all video-conference link witnesses are concluded by this week, including possibly to extend on Friday or -- but could you please try to find out how we would proceed in such a way that we do not waste all the efforts that were made to hear the testimony through videolink. Then I'll not insist on an answer. But if there is anything which the parties would consider that we would have to know, and we really want to know everything that would disturb the schedule, then do not hesitate to approach Chamber staff even this afternoon. Then we adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, the 10th of March, still at 9.30 in the morning, still in this same courtroom, I, but we'll hear the next evidence through videolink. We stand adjourned.
